name: Storm-2561
iocPatterns: "Malicious ZIP download URL from GitHub (e.g., https://github.com/…/VPN-CLIENT.zip)"
"Replaced or revoked digital signing certificates from Taiyuan Lihua Near Information Technology Co., Ltd."
"Spoofed VPN website URLs mimicking legitimate vendors such as Ivanti, Cisco, and Fortinet"
keyCapabilities: "Distribution of fake VPN installers via malicious ZIP files"
"Exploitation of revoked or fake digital signatures"
"Credential harvesting through UI mimicry of legitimate VPN client"
"Persistence via RunOnce registry entry and custom service"
"Command and Control communication to attacker‑controlled IP 194.76.226.93:8080"
"Use of third‑party malware families such as Malagent and Hyrax"
recommendedActions: Implement web filtering to block malicious ZIP downloads from known malicious GitHub repositories.
Enforce strict verification of downloaded VPN client checksums or signatures against a whitelisted corporate signing authority.
Monitor and restrict modifications to Windows RunOnce registry keys and services for unexpected entries like Pulse.exe or PulseSecureService.exe.
Block outbound traffic to the known attacker‑controlled IP 194.76.226.93 on non‑standard ports (e.g., 8080).
Deploy search engine threat analysis controls to detect SEO poisoning patterns related to VPN keyword queries.
Configure endpoint protection solutions to include signatures or heuristics for Malagent and Hyrax backdoors.
Set up registry anomaly detection for boot‑time persistence mechanisms such as RunOnce entries or service installations.
Educate users on verifying VPN client origins and reporting suspicious installation prompts.
campaignsText: Storm‑2561 has been active since at least May 2025, deploying a single, reusable SEO poisoning framework that redirects users across multiple legitimate vendor sites (Ivanti, Cisco, Fortinet). The group hosts malicious payloads on compromised or newly created GitHub repositories and uses a combination of RunOnce registry entries and bootable services for persistence. Exfiltration is consolidated to a single IP address, simplifying detection but also indicating limited operational sophistication in C2 management. Victims span a wide range of industries and countries; the actor regularly changes hosting domains and certificate details to evade reputation checks. The campaign’s speed—from initial poisoning to credential theft—suggests automated tooling and an emphasis on mass monetization over targeted espionage.
description: Storm‑2561 is a financially motivated cybercriminal group leveraging SEO poisoning to entice users searching for VPN software into downloading malicious ZIP files that contain fraudulently signed fake VPN clients. The operation harvests credentials, establishes persistence via RunOnce registry entries or services, and exfiltrates data through an attacker‑controlled IP. Their technique mix targets a broad spectrum of sectors across multiple countries, including government, defense, healthcare, finance, media, and non‑profits.
goals: Storm‑2561’s objective is primarily monetary gain through large‑scale corporate credential theft. By targeting high‑profile industries—government, defense, finance, healthcare, hospitality, think‑tanks and media—they seek credentials that grant access to sensitive systems or financial transactions. The broad geographic reach spanning the US, Russia, North Korea, India, and Indonesia indicates a strategy of opportunistic targeting rather than narrow geopolitical objectives. Their operational tempo reflects efficient campaign execution: SEO poisoning is low maintenance, the malware leverages reusable scripts (RunOnce, service persistence), and all exfiltration funnels through a single C2 host, simplifying command and control.
